title: What If the Sky Rained Candy?

props.title: What if the sky rained candy?

shots.say: What if candy fell from the sky? At first, it would look magical.
shots.what: What if candy fell from the sky? At first, it would look magical.

shots.say: Jelly beans would bounce off the grass and pile up everywhere.
shots.what: Jelly beans would bounce off the grass and pile up everywhere.

props.label: Real clouds
props.sub: Tiny water drops and ice crystals

shots.say: But real clouds are made of tiny water drops and ice. Candy would take magic.
shots.what: But real clouds are made of tiny water drops and ice. Candy would take magic.

shots.say: Falling candy speeds up until air drag balances gravity. Size and shape set that speed.
shots.what: Falling candy speeds up until air drag balances gravity. Size and shape set that speed.

shots.say: Hard sweets could sting. Soft gummies would just splat.
shots.what: Hard sweets could sting. Soft gummies would just splat.

shots.say: Then real rain would melt the sugar into sticky syrup, flowing into drains.
shots.what: Then real rain would melt the sugar into sticky syrup, flowing into drains.

props.label: Used up
props.sub: Microbes eating sugar use the oxygen fish need

shots.say: In streams, microbes eating that sugar would use up oxygen that fish need.
shots.what: In streams, microbes eating that sugar would use up oxygen that fish need.

shots.say: Magical at first. Sticky for much longer. Would you try it?
shots.what: Magical at first. Sticky for much longer. Would you try it?

youtube.title: What If the Sky Rained Candy? 🍬
youtube.description: Jelly beans falling from the sky sounds like a dream. But what would happen next? From air drag to sticky streams, here is the sweet (and sticky) science. The candy storm is imaginary; the science is real.

sources.name: NOAA — Clouds
sources.claim: Cloud particles are tiny water droplets and/or ice crystals.

sources.name: NASA Glenn — Terminal velocity
sources.claim: A falling object stops speeding up when drag equals weight; area and shape (drag coefficient) set that speed.

sources.name: USGS — Dissolved oxygen and water
sources.claim: Aquatic life needs dissolved oxygen; bacteria use oxygen as organic matter decays.
